title: Are evil spirits God’s officers or bands of robbers?
source_text: Δεῖται δὲ καὶ εἰς τὸ τέτακται δὲ ἐφ᾿ ἑκάστῳ δύναμιν λαχὼν τοῦ μεγίστου θεοῦ ὅστις ἠξίωται οὑτινοσοῦν ἔργου πάνυ βαθυτέρας ἐπιστήμης καὶ δυναμένης παραστῆσαι. πότερόν ποτε ὡς οἱ δήμιοι ἐν ταῖς πόλεσι καὶ οἱ τεταγμένοι ἐπὶ τῶν σκυθρωπῶν μὲν ἀναγκαίων δὲ ἐν ταῖς πολιτείαις πραγμάτων οὕτως εἰσὶ τεταγμένοι μοχθηροὶ δαίμονες ἐπί τινων ὑπὸ τοῦ διοικοῦντος τὰ ὅλα λόγου θεοῦ, ἢ ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν ταῖς ἐρημίαις λῃστεύοντες καὶ ἕνα τινὰ προστησάμενοι ἄρχειν αὐτῶν οὕτως οἱ δαίμονες οἱονεὶ κατὰ τόπους τῆς γῆς συστήματα γενόμενοι ἄρχοντά τινα ἑαυτοῖς πεποιήκασι, τὸν ἡγησόμενον αὐτῶν εἰς τὰς πράξεις, ἃς εἵλαντο ὑπὲρ τοῦ κλέπτειν καὶ λῃστεύειν ἀνθρώπων ψυχάς. χρεία δὲ τῷ μέλλοντι εἰς ταῦτα λέγειν καλῶς. ἵνα περὶ Χριστιανῶν ἀπολογήσηται, ἐκτρεπομένων ἄλλο τι σέβειν παρὰ τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν καὶ τὸν πρωτότοκον „πάσης κτίσεως“ λόγον αὐτοῦ. διηγήσασθαι καὶ τὸ „πάντες, ὅσοι ἦλθον πρὸ ἐμοῦ. κλέπται εἰσὶ καὶ λῃσταὶ. καὶ οὐκ ἤκουσεν αὐτῶν τὰ πρόβατα“ καὶ τὸ „ὁ κλέπτης οὐκ ἔρχεται. εἰ μὴ ἵνα κλέψῃ καὶ θύσῃ καὶ ἀπολέσῃ,“ καὶ εἴ τι ἄλλο τούτοις εἴρηται παραπλήσιον ἐν τοῖς ἱεροῖς γράμμασιν, ὥσπερ καὶ τὸ „ἰδοὺ δέδωκα ὑμῖν ἐξουσίαν πατεῖν ἐπάνω ὄφεων καὶ σκορπίων καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ ἐχθροῦ, καὶ οὐδὲν ὑμᾶς οὐ μὴ ἀδικήσῃ“ καὶ τὸ „ἐπ᾿ ἀσπίδα καὶ βασιλίσκον ἐπιβήσῃ καὶ καταπατήσεις λέοντα καὶ δράκοντα.“ ἀλλ᾿ οὐδαμῶς ᾔδει ταῦτα ὁ Κέλσος· εἰ γὰρ ᾔδει, οὐκ ἂν εἶπε· καὶ ὅ τι περ ἂν ᾖ ἐν τοῖς ὅλοις. εἴτε θεοῦ ἔργον εἴτ᾿ ἀγγέων εἴτ᾿ ἄλλων δαιμόνων εἴτε ἡρώων, ταῦτ᾿ ἔχει νόμον ἐκ τοῦ μεγίστου θεοῦ, τέτακται δὲ ἐφ᾿ ἑκάστῳ δύναμιν λαχὼν ὅστις ἠξίωται; τοῦτον οὖν τὸν ἐκεῖθεν ἐξουσίας τετυχηκότα οὐ θεραπεύσει δικαίως ὁ σέβων τὸν θεόν; τούτοις δ᾿ ἐπιφέρει τὸ οὐ γὰρ οἷόν τε „δουλεύειν“ τὸν αὐτὸν πλείοσι „κυρίοις“· περὶ οὗ ἐν τῷ ἑξῆς βιβλίῳ διαληψόμεθα. ἅτε αὐτάρκη περιγραφὴν εἰληφότος τοῦ ἑβδόμου τόμου, πρὸς τὸ σύγγραμμα Κέλσου ἡμῖν γεγραμμένου.
pass_a_gloss: it needs (δεῖται) also, for [the clause] 'is appointed (τέτακται) over each, having received by lot power from the greatest God, whoever has been deemed worthy (ὅστις ἠξίωται) of any work (ἔργον) whatever', a much deeper knowledge and one able to set forth/prove (παραστῆσαι): whether (πότερον) as the public executioners (δήμιοι) in cities and those appointed (τεταγμένοι) over gloomy (σκυθρωπά) but necessary (ἀναγκαῖα) affairs (πράγματα) in states (πολιτεῖαι), so wicked demons are appointed over certain things by the Word of God (λόγος θεοῦ) who administers the whole; or (ἤ) as those robbing (λῃστεύοντες) in deserts (ἐρημίαι) and having set over themselves (προστησάμενοι) one man to rule (ἄρχειν) them, so the demons, as it were (οἱονεί) in regions of the earth having become companies/bands, have made a certain ruler (ἄρχων) for themselves, the one to lead (ἡγησόμενον) them into the deeds (πράξεις) which they chose (εἵλαντο) for stealing and plundering souls of men. there is need (χρεία) for the one about to (μέλλοντι) speak well (καλῶς) on these things, so that he may make defence (ἀπολογήσηται) for Christians, who turn aside from (ἐκτρεπομένων) worshipping (σέβειν) anything else beside (παρά) the God over all (ἐπὶ πᾶσι) and His Word (λόγος), the firstborn of all creation, to expound (διηγήσασθαι) also 'all who came before me are thieves (κλέπται) and robbers (λῃσταί), and the sheep (πρόβατα) did not hear them' and 'the thief (κλέπτης) does not come except to steal (κλέψῃ) and slaughter (θύσῃ) and destroy (ἀπολέσῃ)', and whatever else similar (παραπλήσιον) to these is said in the sacred writings, as also 'behold (ἰδού) I have given you authority (ἐξουσία) to tread (πατεῖν) upon serpents (ὄφεις) and scorpions (σκορπίοι) and upon all the power of the enemy, and nothing by no means (οὐ μή) will harm (ἀδικήσῃ) you' and 'upon asp (ἀσπίς) and basilisk (βασιλίσκος) you will step (ἐπιβήσῃ), and trample (καταπατήσεις) lion (λέων) and dragon (δράκων)'. ἀλλ' but by no means knew (οὐδαμῶς ᾔδει) these Celsus; for if he had known, he would not have said: 'and whatever may be in the universe (ἐν τοῖς ὅλοις), whether work of God or of angels or of other demons or of heroes (ἥρωες), these have a law (ἔχει νόμον) from the greatest God, and appointed over each, having been allotted power, is whoever has been deemed worthy. this one then (τοῦτον οὖν), who has obtained authority from there, shall not the one revering God justly serve/worship?' To these he adds (ἐπιφέρει) 'for it is not possible (οἷόν τε) to be a slave to (δουλεύειν) the same man to more lords/masters'; about which (περὶ οὗ) in the next book (ἑξῆς βιβλίον) we shall treat (διαληψόμεθα), since (ἅτε) the seventh volume (ἕβδομος τόμος), written by us against Celsus's treatise, has taken a sufficient compass.
pass_b_english: The words “and whoever has been deemed worthy of any task at all has been appointed over each, having been allotted power by the greatest God” also need a far deeper knowledge, one able to show which is the case. Are wicked demons appointed over certain things by the Word of God who governs the universe, in the way that executioners in cities, and those appointed over grim but necessary business in states, are appointed? Or, just as robbers in the wilderness set up one man to rule them, have the demons, as it were, formed bands in different regions of the earth and made themselves a ruler, to lead them in the deeds they have chosen, deeds aimed at stealing and plundering the souls of men?

Whoever means to speak well on these questions, so as to defend the Christians, who turn away from worshipping anything other than the God over all and His Word, “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), needs also to explain the saying, “All who came before me are thieves and robbers, and the sheep did not hear them” (John 10:8), and the saying, “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy” (John 10:10), and anything else like these that is said in the sacred writings, such as, “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall ever harm you” (Luke 10:19), and, “You shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 91:13).

But Celsus knew nothing at all of these things; for had he known them, he would not have said: “And whatever there is in the universe, whether the work of God or of angels or of other demons or of heroes, these things have a law from the greatest God, and whoever has been deemed worthy has been appointed over each, having been allotted power. Shall not, then, the one who worships God rightly serve this being, who has obtained his authority from that source?”

To these words he adds, “For it is not possible for the same man to serve many masters” (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13). We shall treat this in the next book, since this seventh volume, which we have written in answer to Celsus’s treatise, has now reached a sufficient length.

choices.choice: Celsus’s words are those first quoted at 7.68 (“and whatever there is in the universe ... has a law from the greatest God ...”); at 7.70 the staged text drops πάντα before ταῦτα, and I translate it as staged. Staged text reads ἀγγέων, a typo for ἀγγέλων (“of angels”), as 7.68 has it; translated as ἀγγέλων. The staged punctuation puts a Greek question mark (;) after ἠξίωται, carried over from 7.68, where Celsus phrases the whole as a string of rhetorical questions opened by οὐ; this re-quotation begins after that οὐ, so I render the first sentence as a statement and the second (τοῦτον οὖν ... ὁ σέβων τὸν θεόν;) as a question; the sense is the same either way. I take οὐκ ἂν εἶπε to govern both sentences of Celsus. λόγου θεοῦ with διοικοῦντος τὰ ὅλα is read as “the Word of God who governs the universe” (the participle agrees with λόγου). οὑτινοσοῦν ἔργου is taken with ἠξίωται (“deemed worthy of any task at all”); it could also be read with ἐφ’ ἑκάστῳ (“over each work whatever”). πότερον ... ἤ is rendered “which is the case” followed by the two questions. θύσῃ in John 10:10 is rendered “kill” (literally “slaughter, sacrifice”). οὐδὲν ὑμᾶς οὐ μὴ ἀδικήσῃ (Luke 10:19) keeps the emphatic double negative as “nothing shall ever harm you”. LXX Psalm 90:13 = English Psalm 91:13 (LXX “asp and basilisk ... lion and dragon”; kept as Origen quotes). The “many masters” saying is Celsus’s use of the Gospel saying, Matthew 6:24 (parallel Luke 16:13), cited as at 7.68; the staged Greek marks only δουλεύειν and κυρίοις as Gospel words, but the whole clause is Celsus’s, so the whole is quoted; at 7.68 Origen marks it with φησί. δαίμονες rendered “demons”, matching 7.68-7.69 and the rest of the work; Origen treats all demons as fallen (7.69). No classical quotation in this chapter.
"daemons" changed to "demons" to match 7.68-7.69 and the work as a whole (449 vs 38 uses)
Opening quoted clause reordered from Greek word order ("there is appointed ... whoever") to natural English; same in Celsus's re-quotation
"Celsus's statement" changed to "The words": the Greek (εἰς τό) names no speaker
"able to show the truth of the matter" changed to "able to show which is the case" to reflect πότερον ... ἤ instead of adding a phrase
"some one man" changed to "one man"; "made a ruler for themselves" to "made themselves a ruler"; "places" to "regions" for κατὰ τόπους
Restored εἴρηται: "anything else like these that is said in the sacred writings"
Restored γάρ: "for had he known them"
Celsus's second question aligned with the 7.68 rendering ("Shall not, then, the one who worships God rightly serve this being ...")
Added Luke 16:13 beside Matthew 6:24, as at 7.68
Title: "a band" changed to "bands" (the demons form bands in many places)
